transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-18 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Emma Chen (Crestline CTO), Luis Martinez (Lead ML Engineer), Sara Park (Product)

Summary (auto): quick hosted-API demo, cover streaming and params, next steps for POC

00:00 Jordan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood, and with me is Priya from our solutions engineering team. How's everyone doing?
00:07 Emma (Crestline): Good thanks, excited to see this. We want to understand how quickly we can get chat summarization into our customer support flow and what the latency looks like.
00:16 Jordan: Great, goal for today is a short walkthrough of the Hosted API for chat/text generation basics - streaming, params like temperature, top_p, max_tokens, and our recommendations for retries and production safety. We'll keep it practical.
00:28 Priya (Redwood SE): Quick note on agenda: one, show a curl + python SDK example; two, demo streaming so you see tokens as they arrive; three, talk about param tuning and cost/latency tradeoffs; four, retries and idempotency; five, Q&A and next steps.
00:44 Luis (Crestline): Sounds good. Our main constraints: sub-500ms median for single-turn replies would be ideal but we'll take 1s, and we need PII controls - data residency and logs retention.
00:55 Jordan: Totally understood. We can cover those security bits and share our compliance pack. For latency, hosted API usually depends on model choice and prompt length - we have verified profiles for common models in our catalog.
01:10 Priya: Alright I'll share my screen - demo app. First example is a simple chat request using curl. Note that our chat endpoint supports system, user, assistant roles and streaming via server-sent events. Example curl snippet: 

curl -X POST https://api.redwood.inference/v1/chat 
 -H 'Authorization: Bearer <KEY>' 
 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' 
 -d '{"messages":[{"role":"system","content":"You are a helpful assistant."},{"role":"user","content":"Summarize the order notes for order #1234"}], "stream": true, "max_tokens": 150, "temperature": 0.2}'

01:50 Priya: With stream: true you'll get partial tokens as events. That helps with perceived latency in UI. We also support websocket streams if you need two-way flows.
02:05 Emma: Does stream impact cost?
02:08 Priya: Not directly - cost is per-token generated. Streaming just changes delivery; you still pay for tokens produced. However, perceived latency improves because you don't wait for the full generation.
02:20 Luis: What about token counting? We have lot of long prompts including product catalogs.
02:24 Priya: We count input + output tokens. Max_tokens caps the output. We recommend prefixing system messages carefully and using retrieval-based short context to keep prompt sizes down. Also we can suggest quantization/model variants if you need lower cost per token.
02:40 Jordan: We'll share examples of token accounting and a simple cost calc sheet after the call.
02:48 Priya: Next, params: temperature controls randomness - 0.0-1.0, typical values 0.0-0.3 for deterministic summarization, 0.7+ for creative copy. top_p is nucleus sampling; you can use together but we recommend tuning one at a time. max_tokens caps output length. Stop sequences can be set for stable terminations.
03:20 Priya: Quick demo of adjusting temperature - watch how the paraphrase changes slightly. Also show function calling / structured output: you can ask model to return JSON and validate in your app. Note: function calling is model dependent - some models have explicit function call support.
03:50 Emma: Could you talk about retries? We have flaky clients and load balancers in front of our services.
03:56 Priya: Good question - for safety we recommend using idempotency keys on create-like requests and an exponential backoff with jitter for transient 5xx or 429 responses. Redwood returns helpful error codes: 429 for rate limit, 5xx for server error, 4xx for client issues. Example: if you get a 429, backoff and retry up to 3 times, use the Retry-After header if provided.
04:30 Luis: Any guidance for exactly-once vs at-least-once?
04:33 Priya: Use idempotency key if the downstream operation is non-idempotent. For pure generation calls that are read-only, you can safely retry, but for combined flows that log or charge, use your own idempotency layer.
04:50 Jordan: Also note our SDK includes helpers for retries with exponential backoff; you'll get sensible defaults you can override.
05:00 Priya: Now I'll show the python SDK example for chat (short).

from redwood import Client
client = Client(api_key=\"<KEY>\")
resp = client.chat.create(messages=[{\"role\":\"system\",\"content\":\"You are concise.\"},{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"Create a 2-sentence product blurb for a waterproof jacket.\"}], stream=True, temperature=0.1)

05:30 Priya: If stream=True in the SDK you'll get an iterator of events - each yields partial content, and you can render tokens as they arrive.
05:40 Emma: For production what patterns should we use for batching or concurrency?
05:44 Priya: For user-facing single-turn queries, keep concurrency per-model modest to avoid queueing. For high throughput, use batching or Redwood Optimize recommendations - we can suggest batching size and quantized model variants based on your traffic pattern. For real-time chat, small batch sizes or single-request lanes are typical.
06:10 Luis: We also want to do multi-turn with KV cache to keep context without resending everything. Does Redwood keep KV cache on Hosted?
06:18 Priya: Short answer: yes - the runtime manages KV cache for autoregressive decoding to speed up token generation. If you do private deployments you can pin more aggressive caching policies. In Hosted we manage cache and it's tuned by model and seq-length. Sometimes logs will show 'K V cache evicted' in our traces - small transcription note: logs might appear as KV cache or 'K V cache' depending on parser.
06:42 Jordan: Switching gears, rate limiting and quotas. Hosted accounts have default rate limits; if you need higher throughput we can open dedicated capacity or reserved pools. Dedicated gives you predictable latency and throughput guarantees.
06:55 Emma: What about data retention and logs for compliance?
07:00 Jordan: Our Hosted API has configurable retention. By default we retain short-term logs for debugging, but for enterprise we offer options to disable retention and send logs to your SIEM, plus support for SSO, RBAC, and KMS integrations. We'll share the SOC2 and security whitepaper.
07:22 Sara (Crestline): Any gotchas around streaming and mobile clients?
07:26 Priya: Mobile can benefit a lot from streaming for perceived latency, but you need to handle partial message concatenation and reconnection. Use idempotency keys and resume logic on reconnects; for resumable streams we recommend websocket with a short keepalive.
07:45 Priya: Quick perf note - smaller models are faster; higher temperature doesn't change latency much but can increase token count slightly because of retries in sampling. Also reducing max_tokens or using early stop sequences saves cost.
08:05 Jordan: Let's show a short live example against a small demo model to see streaming. (Priya starts request)
08:18 Transcript: [streaming tokens appear] \"We reviewed your order notes, items: 2 x jackets, shipping expedited...\" (partial tokens)
08:40 Emma: That looks useful. Latency looked under a second in this demo.
08:45 Priya: Demo environment is small, production numbers will vary. We'll run a small benchmark for you with your prompts.
09:00 Jordan: Questions on error handling?
09:04 Luis: How do you handle partial responses if the stream disconnects mid-generation?
09:08 Priya: Client should have logic to detect truncated events; you can either retry with same idempotency key and a flag to continue or re-ask with the partial text as context. We also log chunk offsets which helps in debugging.
09:26 Emma: Pricing? Ballpark per-token numbers or comparisons to other providers?
09:30 Jordan: We'll send a pricing sheet - public mentions aside, per-token pricing depends on model family. We also show unit economics: tokens per request, average tokens/month, and options like model quantization or Dedicated to lower per-token latency/cost.
09:50 Luis: Competitors - we looked at OpenAI and Anthropic; how's Redwood different?
09:55 Jordan: Redwood focuses on serving and ops - unified runtime across Hosted/Dedicated/Private, transparent perf profiles per model, and tooling like Redwood Optimize for batching/cost suggestions. Customers pick us when they want predictable production inference economics rather than experimenting with infra.
10:12 Priya: Anything else on architecture or infra?
10:16 Luis: For POC, we'd probably run hosted first, then consider Dedicated if latency/cost needs justify it. Timeline: 2-3 week POC, then decision.
10:26 Jordan: Perfect. Next steps recap: Jordan will send pricing + SLA and security docs; Priya will run a quick latency benchmark and share results; Emma will share sample prompts and a small anonymized dataset. We'll schedule POC kickoff once those are in place.
10:45 Emma: Thanks - that works.
10:49 Jordan: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs.
